P1.evidence: The setter handover was genuinely used, three separate times — 'I saw that in the application, you felt it was an 8', 'I also heard something from Kim around youth parts' and 'I also saw the questions that you send in'. The frame covered goals, current position and whether the programme fits, with an explicit disqualification offer, but no 'what's in the way' or 'what you need' element. Agreement was taken twice, on time ('are you okay with that time?') and on the frame ('okay?' — 'Okay. Perfect.'). Open question landed cleanly.

P2.evidence: Age, height and weight asked directly and immediately. Injuries were the strongest section — he picked up the knees and lower back from the application and probed duration properly: 'what's quite a while, is that like a year? five years'. Diet asked well. But work was never asked about at all: the two full-time jobs and the overnight shift only surfaced at 00:26:00 when the prospect volunteered them as the reason he could train. Health conditions never asked. Sleep never asked, which on a man working 12:30pm-9pm then 10pm-6am is the single most costly omission in the call. Energy never asked. The training split came out only in answer to a different question.

P3.evidence: 'Describe that 10 out of the 10 version of a Tyler for me' produced a detailed picture. The can't-do-it question ran and worked: 'do you feel like it also maybe has an effect on your life where you're not able to do everything that you want to do?' drew out sprinting and box jumps. The emotional question was the best moment of the call — 'how do you think you would feel in your body when you have that confidence you can actually take off your shirt?' produced 'a weight off of my shoulders' and the devil-and-angel image the rep then built on. But the bridge out of the physical was fed to him from the setter notes rather than asked open, 'Who else does that impact?' was never asked — family and role model came unprompted — and no reflect-back reframe was ever made.

P4.evidence: The history of years of traditional bodybuilding and repeated weight cycling was volunteered rather than asked for, and never probed for what specifically happened each time. The root cause questions ran well and in sequence — 'What do you feel like is getting in the way of actually finding that right formula for yourself?' followed by 'What do you think that you haven't made that full switch yet?' and 'Why, why now?' — and the prospect named the gap himself: diet, plus a training method that had given him the frame but not the result. The scripted 'the information isn't the problem' line never ran.

P5.evidence: The consequence question ran in the prospect's own metaphor and produced the strongest material in the transcript: 'let's skip forward a year, you choose for the devil... where do you think you would be in like a year, two, three years from now?' returned 'I feel like I can't afford to listen to the devil on the shoulder... it's going to feel like I'm closing in on 40 and it's going to feel like it's too late'. The line-in-the-sand equivalent also ran: 'Do you feel like you are actually ready to rewound the clock?'. But he was never asked whether he was willing to settle for it, or why not — the prospect supplied both unprompted, which the script credits asking for, not receiving.

P6.evidence: The belief question ran cleanly before anything was presented: 'let's say you have that structure for yourself. You have that accountability. You have someone in your corner... do you feel like you're then actually going to be able to follow through?' The all-in question was never asked in its scripted form; the nearest was 'is this something I see myself starting with or do you have any more questions on it?', which returned a yes immediately qualified by budget. He addressed that qualification with a good pre-isolation ('even if you have all the money in the world... there's no use case in starting with it, unless you actually see it working') but then went straight to the number rather than returning to Phase 5.

P11.evidence: Payment was attempted and partially collected — $100 of $6,000, taken live by card, with the financing deferred to the next day. The Trevor onboarding call was proposed for Thursday but not booked on the call: 'then tomorrow we do the financing and we can book in a meeting with Trevor for on Thursday'. No agreement email was mentioned or signed, and nothing was said about the welcome email, the Skool community link or the onboarding questionnaire. The recording ends mid card capture so even step 1 is not evidenced as complete.

objection_plays.detail: The fullest money play in this batch, and still incomplete. What ran: a pre-price isolation on belief; the open-conversation ask, near-verbatim — 'If you want, we can have an open conversation about it. Just see if we can make something work'; cash on hand, asked three separate ways ('what would you be able to basically get started with today', 'what is something that is currently on your account'); and monthly surplus, which returned 'maybe $500 a month'. What did not run: the 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place' reframe; the 'most clients pay upfront, but for some we break it up' line; and four of the six financial-picture questions — number of credit cards, available credit per card, used versus available, and any investments. A credit-score question was substituted, which is not in the play, and it was used to qualify him for third-party financing rather than to map what he already had.

The prospect raised a third-party funder — his father had asked what he wanted for his 35th birthday and might contribute. There is no scripted play for a parent or third party as a funding source, as distinct from a spouse whose permission is being sought. The rep parked it entirely ('you can then have that conversation about the rest of your dad') and never returned to it, so a live and willing source of the balance was left unworked while $100 was extracted from a credit card instead.

notes: Discovery and the consequence frame were the best work in this batch — he used the prospect's own devil-and-angel metaphor to drive urgency, and the setter handover was properly used. Two things undo it. Baseline skipped work, health conditions, sleep and energy on a man doing two full-time jobs and an overnight shift, so the plan was built without knowing when he sleeps. And at the close he converted a strong money play into a $100 credit-card deposit from someone who had just said he had nothing until payday, rather than working the father, the payday twenty-four hours away, or a structure the prospect could actually carry.
